claim: TBC1D15 is a mitochondrial Rab GTPase-activating protein (Rab-GAP) that governs autophagosome biogenesis and morphology downstream of Parkin activation.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that TBC1D15, a mitochondrial Rab GTPase-activating protein (Rab-GAP), governs autophagosome biogenesis and morphology downstream of Parkin activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing TBC1D15's role in mitophagy.

claim: TBC1D15 inhibits Rab7 activity to constrain autophagosome morphogenesis to that of the cargo.
source: To constrain autophagosome morphogenesis to that of the cargo, TBC1D15 inhibits Rab7 activity and associates with both the mitochondria through binding Fis1 and the isolation membrane through the interactions with LC3/GABARAP family members.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing Rab7 knockdown suppresses LC3 accumulation in TBC1D15-/- cells and that TBC1D15 GAP activity is required.

claim: TBC1D15 associates with mitochondria through binding Fis1.
source: To constrain autophagosome morphogenesis to that of the cargo, TBC1D15 inhibits Rab7 activity and associates with both the mitochondria through binding Fis1 and the isolation membrane through the interactions with LC3/GABARAP family members.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing TBC1D15 localization to mitochondria and binding assays with Fis1.

claim: TBC1D15 associates with the isolation membrane through interactions with LC3/GABARAP family members.
source: To constrain autophagosome morphogenesis to that of the cargo, TBC1D15 inhibits Rab7 activity and associates with both the mitochondria through binding Fis1 and the isolation membrane through the interactions with LC3/GABARAP family members.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing TBC1D15 binding to LC3/GABARAP proteins through LIR motifs.

claim: TBC1D17 participates in mitophagy and forms homodimers and heterodimers with TBC1D15.
source: Another TBC family member TBC1D17, also participates in mitophagy and forms homodimers and heterodimers with TBC1D15.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 interactions.

claim: TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 mediate proper autophagic encapsulation of mitochondria by regulating Rab7 activity at the interface between mitochondria and isolation membranes.
source: These results demonstrate that TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 mediate proper autophagic encapsulation of mitochondria by regulating Rab7 activity at the interface between mitochondria and isolation membranes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the role of TBC1D15/17 in mitophagy and Rab7 regulation.

claim: PINK1 and Parkin play a central role in triggering mitophagy in mammals.
source: Although two gene products mutated in Parkinson's disease, PINK1, and Parkin have been found to play a central role in triggering mitophagy in mammals, how the pre-autophagosomal isolation membrane selectively and accurately engulfs damaged mitochondria remains unclear.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and cited literature.

claim: Cup-shaped isolation membranes surround cytosol and organelles upon starvation.
source: Cup-shaped isolation membranes surround cytosol and organelles upon starvation (Baba et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: During xenophagy, autophagosomes form locally on the surface of the substrate and grow in contour with irregularly shaped structures.
source: However, when large aggregates of debris accumulate or during xenophagy (Kageyama et al., 2011), autophagosomes form locally on the surface of the substrate and grow in contour with the often irregularly shaped structures that can be much larger than the membrane cups formed during starvation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: For large aggregates of mitochondria, several autophagosomes may form simultaneously on different sides of the cargo and fuse together to engulf them.
source: Furthermore, for large aggregates of mitochondria, several autophagosomes may form simultaneously on different sides of the cargo and fuse together to engulf them (Yoshii et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TBC1D15 has been shown to bind mitochondria through Fis1.
source: TBC1D15 has been shown to bind mitochondria through Fis1 (Onoue et al., 2013), to bind the Atg8 family member GABARAP (Behrends et al., 2010), and has been found in a screen of Parkin substrates (Sarraf et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TBC1D15 has been shown to bind the Atg8 family member GABARAP.
source: TBC1D15 has been shown to bind mitochondria through Fis1 (Onoue et al., 2013), to bind the Atg8 family member GABARAP (Behrends et al., 2010), and has been found in a screen of Parkin substrates (Sarraf et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TBC1D15 has been found in a screen of Parkin substrates.
source: TBC1D15 has been shown to bind mitochondria through Fis1 (Onoue et al., 2013), to bind the Atg8 family member GABARAP (Behrends et al., 2010), and has been found in a screen of Parkin substrates (Sarraf et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TBC1D15 is one of the TBC (Tre-2/Bub2/Cdc16) family proteins that function as Rab GTPase-activating proteins (Rab-GAPs).
source: TBC1D15 is one of the TBC (Tre-2/Bub2/Cdc16) family proteins that function as Rab GTPase-activating proteins (Rab-GAPs) (Fukuda, 2011; Frasa et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Fis1 is C-terminally anchored in the mitochondrial outer membrane.
source: Fis1, conserved from yeast to mammals, is C-terminally anchored in the mitochondrial outer membrane (Mozdy et al., 2000) with an N-terminal tetratricopeptide-repeat (TPR) domain exposed to the cytosol (Suzuki et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Fis1 has an N-terminal tetratricopeptide-repeat (TPR) domain exposed to the cytosol.
source: Fis1, conserved from yeast to mammals, is C-terminally anchored in the mitochondrial outer membrane (Mozdy et al., 2000) with an N-terminal tetratricopeptide-repeat (TPR) domain exposed to the cytosol (Suzuki et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Fis1 knock out mammalian cells do not display a defect in mitochondrial fission.
source: Although mammalian Fis1 had been thought to be a mitochondrial fission factor in the same way as yeast Fis1, Fis1 knock out mammalian cells do not display a defect in mitochondrial fission (Otera et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Mammalian Drp1 recruitment to mitochondria requires Mff, MIEF1/MiD51, and/or MiD49.
source: Also in contrast to yeast, mammalian Drp1 recruitment to mitochondria requires Mff, MIEF1/MiD51, and/or MiD49 (Otera et al., 2010; Palmer et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Fis1 null worm and Fis1 knock out mammalian cells have excessive LC3 accumulation following stress induced by mitochondrial inhibitors such as antimycin A in a PINK1-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, the Fis1 null worm and Fis1 knock out mammalian cells have excessive LC3 accumulation following stress induced by mitochondrial inhibitors such as antimycin A in a PINK1-dependent manner (Shen et al., 2014) suggesting Fis1 may have a role in mitophagy.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A TBC1D15 gene knock out (KO) cell line was made using TALENs.
source: As TBC1D15 binds to Fis1 (Onoue et al., 2013) and is a Rab-GAP potentially involved in autophagy (Behrends et al., 2010), we made a TBC1D15 gene knock out (KO) cell line using TALENs (Transcription activator-like effector nucleases [Gaj et al., 2013]) and compared the LC3 accumulation phenotype with that of FIS1−/− cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data describing the generation of the cell line.

claim: One TBC1D15−/− clone harbors a 14-bp deletion in one allele and a large deletion in the other allele, both of which are frame-shifting and would cause mRNA decay.
source: One TBC1D15−/− clone harbors a 14-bp deletion in one allele and a large deletion in the other allele, both of which are frame-shifting and would cause mRNA decay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The knock out of TBC1D15 expression was confirmed by immunoblotting.
source: We confirmed the knock out of TBC1D15 expression by immunoblotting (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Each KO cell line has complete deletion of the target protein, but expression and/or stability of the other fission-related proteins was not affected.
source: Although each KO cell line has complete deletion of the target protein, expression and/or stability of the other fission-related proteins was not affected; FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells possess normal levels of TBC1D15 and Fis1, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells possess normal levels of TBC1D15 and Fis1, respectively.
source: Although each KO cell line has complete deletion of the target protein, expression and/or stability of the other fission-related proteins was not affected; FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells possess normal levels of TBC1D15 and Fis1, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mitochondrial morphology in FIS1−/− cells was similar to that of WT cells.
source: In agreement with previous work (Otera et al., 2010), mitochondrial morphology, as well as peroxisomal morphology in FIS1−/− cells, was similar to that of WT cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and cited literature.

claim: Peroxisomal morphology in FIS1−/− cells was similar to that of WT cells.
source: In agreement with previous work (Otera et al., 2010), mitochondrial morphology, as well as peroxisomal morphology in FIS1−/− cells, was similar to that of WT cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and cited literature.

claim: Complete depletion of TBC1D15 by knock out resulted in no obvious mitochondrial morphology changes.
source: In contrast to moderately elongated mitochondria in TBC1D15 siRNA-treated cells reported previously (Onoue et al., 2013), complete depletion of TBC1D15 by knock out resulted in no obvious mitochondrial morphology changes (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Peroxisome shape in TBC1D15−/− cells was indistinguishable from that of WT cells.
source: Furthermore, peroxisome shape in TBC1D15−/− cells was also indistinguishable from that of WT cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MFF−/− and DRP−/− cells display elongated mitochondria and peroxisomes.
source: In sharp contrast, MFF−/− and DRP−/− cells display elongated mitochondria and peroxisomes (Figure 1B), indicating that Mff and Drp1 play important roles in regulating both mitochondria and peroxisome morphology, consistent with the previous findings (Smirnova et al., 1998; Koch et al., 2003; Gandre-Babbe and van der Bliek, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and cited literature.

claim: Mff and Drp1 play important roles in regulating both mitochondria and peroxisome morphology.
source: In sharp contrast, MFF−/− and DRP−/− cells display elongated mitochondria and peroxisomes (Figure 1B), indicating that Mff and Drp1 play important roles in regulating both mitochondria and peroxisome morphology, consistent with the previous findings (Smirnova et al., 1998; Koch et al., 2003; Gandre-Babbe and van der Bliek, 2008).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data and supported by cited literature.

claim: The fission defect in MFF−/− cells is similar to, but not as strong as, that caused by DRP1 deletion.
source: Quantification of mitochondrial morphology demonstrated that the fission defect in MFF−/− cells is similar to, but not as strong as, that caused by DRP1 deletion (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Both TBC1D15 and Fis1 are dispensable for mitochondrial and peroxisomal fission in human cells.
source: Therefore, it appears that both TBC1D15 and Fis1 are dispensable for mitochondrial and peroxisomal fission in human cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing no morphology changes in TBC1D15−/− and FIS1−/− cells.

claim: FIS1−/− cells accumulate LC3 during Parkin-mediated mitophagy.
source: FIS1−/− cells accumulate LC3 during Parkin-mediated mitophagy (Shen et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: 3 hr of valinomycin treatment to depolarize mitochondria-stimulated Parkin translocation onto mitochondria with similar efficiencies in all cell lines tested.
source: 3 hr of valinomycin treatment to depolarize mitochondria-stimulated Parkin translocation onto mitochondria with similar efficiencies in all cell lines tested (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: WT cells have several small dots, crescent-shaped, or spherical YFP-LC3 puncta representing isolation membranes and autophagosomes that were observed on or near fragmented mitochondria.
source: WT cells have several small dots, crescent-shaped, or spherical YFP-LC3 puncta representing isolation membranes and autophagosomes, respectively, that were observed on or near fragmented mitochondria, consistent with previous observations (Figure 2A and Narendra et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and cited literature.

claim: Upon mitophagy induction in FIS1−/− cells, YFP-LC3 accumulates excessively in foci, which often appears interconnected with one another, localized on or near mitochondria.
source: However, upon mitophagy induction in FIS1−/− cells, YFP-LC3 accumulates excessively in foci, which often appears interconnected with one another, localized on or near mitochondria (Figure 2A,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Shen et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and cited literature.

claim: TBC1D15−/− cells display expanded LC3-labeled structures very similar to those in FIS1−/− cells.
source: Interestingly, TBC1D15−/− cells display expanded LC3-labeled structures very similar to those in FIS1−/− cells suggesting that Fis1 and TBC1D15 are involved at the same step in autophagy (Figure 2A,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fis1 and TBC1D15 are involved at the same step in autophagy.
source: Interestingly, TBC1D15−/− cells display expanded LC3-labeled structures very similar to those in FIS1−/− cells suggesting that Fis1 and TBC1D15 are involved at the same step in autophagy (Figure 2A,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity of phenotypes in FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells.

claim: The LC3 accumulation phenotype in TBC1D15−/− cells requires both Parkin and PINK1 expression and the loss of the inner mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: This phenotype requires both Parkin (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A) and PINK1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B) expression and the loss of the inner mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), indicating that it occurs upon mitophagy induction downstream of PINK1-induced Parkin translocation to mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B,C.

claim: The LC3 accumulation phenotype occurs upon mitophagy induction downstream of PINK1-induced Parkin translocation to mitochondria.
source: This phenotype requires both Parkin (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A) and PINK1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B) expression and the loss of the inner mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), indicating that it occurs upon mitophagy induction downstream of PINK1-induced Parkin translocation to mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing dependence on Parkin, PINK1, and mitochondrial depolarization.

claim: Expression of N-terminally 3×FLAG-tagged Fis1 rescued the LC3 accumulation in FIS1−/− cells.
source: Expression of N-terminally 3×FLAG-tagged Fis1 rescued the LC3 accumulation in FIS1−/− cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), confirming the effect was caused by the loss of Fis1.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: N-terminally HA-tagged WT TBC1D15 expressed in TBC1D15−/− cells reverted the excessive LC3 accumulation to that of WT after mitophagy induction.
source: Similarly, N-terminally HA-tagged WT TBC1D15 expressed in TBC1D15−/− cells reverted the excessive LC3 accumulation to that of WT after mitophagy induction (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Valinomycin treatment for 3 hr caused the formation of preautophagomes with closely apposed membranes that were labeled with gold particles attached to YFP-LC3 near mitochondria in WT cells.
source: Valinomycin treatment for 3 hr caused the formation of preautophagomes with closely apposed membranes that were labeled with gold particles attached to YFP-LC3 near mitochondria in WT cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: TBC1D15−/− cells have cup-shaped membrane structures, many of which displayed much thicker lumens than those in WT cells.
source: Although TBC1D15−/− cells also have similar cup-shaped membrane structures, many of them displayed much thicker lumens than those in WT cells (Figure 2G, panel a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Larger membrane capsules that contain mitochondria and possibly other membrane organelles were observed only in TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: In addition, larger membrane capsules that contain mitochondria and possibly other membrane organelles were observed only in TBC1D15 −/− cells (Figure 2G, panel c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Some LC3 in TBC1D15−/− cells was associated with small diameter membrane structures that localize very close to mitochondria.
source: Furthermore, some LC3 was associated with small diameter membrane structures that localize very close to mitochondria (Figure 2G, panel e) and may have out of plane contiguity to preautophagosomes (Figure 2G, panel e and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The LC3-labeled structures seen in TBC1D15−/− cells are not simply LC3 protein aggregates, but express LC3 associated along membrane bilayers.
source: These results strongly suggest that the LC3-labeled structures seen in TBC1D15−/− cells are not simply LC3 protein aggregates, but express LC3 associated along membrane bilayers.
evidence: The claim is inferred from immunoelectron microscopy data showing membrane-associated LC3.

claim: GFP-ULK1 formed dots and/or cup-shaped structures around mitochondria following valinomycin treatment, although the number of dots did not further increase upon the loss of Fis1 or TBC1D15.
source: GFP-ULK1 that functions in the most upstream ATG1/ULK kinase complex and GFP-Atg14 that is an autophagy specific subunit of the class III PI3K complex formed dots and/or cup-shaped structures around mitochondria following valinomycin treatment, although the number of dots did not further increase upon the loss of Fis1 or TBC1D15 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: GFP-Atg14 formed dots and/or cup-shaped structures around mitochondria following valinomycin treatment, although the number of dots did not further increase upon the loss of Fis1 or TBC1D15.
source: GFP-ULK1 that functions in the most upstream ATG1/ULK kinase complex and GFP-Atg14 that is an autophagy specific subunit of the class III PI3K complex formed dots and/or cup-shaped structures around mitochondria following valinomycin treatment, although the number of dots did not further increase upon the loss of Fis1 or TBC1D15 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Valinomycin induced the formation of both Atg16L1 and DFCP1 dots on mitochondria, but neither of them increased further in FIS1−/− or TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: Although valinomycin induced the formation of both Atg16L1 and DFCP1 dots on mitochondria, neither of them increased further in FIS1−/− or TBC1D15−/− cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Fis1 and TBC1D15 seem to regulate LC3 accumulation downstream of autophagy initiation.
source: Thus, Fis1 and TBC1D15 seem to regulate LC3 accumulation downstream of autophagy initiation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing no increase in early autophagy markers in FIS1−/− or TBC1D15−/− cells.

claim: Upon Parkin-induced mitophagy, TBC1D15−/− cells display more expanded LC3 accumulation than WT cells and also generate thin LC3-labeled tubular structures interconnected to one another.
source: In sharp contrast, upon Parkin-induced mitophagy, TBC1D15−/− cells display more expanded LC3 accumulation than WT cells and also generate thin LC3-labeled tubular structures interconnected to one another, which are very similar to that seen in FIS1 −/− cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by z-stack confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LC3-labeled tubular structures in TBC1D15−/− cells are very similar to that seen in FIS1−/− cells.
source: In sharp contrast, upon Parkin-induced mitophagy, TBC1D15−/− cells display more expanded LC3 accumulation than WT cells and also generate thin LC3-labeled tubular structures interconnected to one another, which are very similar to that seen in FIS1 −/− cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by z-stack confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LC3-labeled tubular structures in TBC1D15−/− cells were frequently observed near the cell cortex.
source: These tubular structures were frequently observed near the cell cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy observations.

claim: The LC3-containing tubules emanating from the LC3 foci are highly mobile.
source: Live cell imaging showed that the LC3-containing tubules emanating from the LC3 foci are highly mobile (Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Video 1.

claim: Long YFP-LC3-labeled tubules observed in TBC1D15−/− cells are membrane associated.
source: Immunoelectron microscopy confirmed that long YFP-LC3-labeled tubules observed in TBC1D15−/− cells are membrane associated (Figure 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LC3-labeled tubules in TBC1D15−/− cells were not associated with ER or actin filaments.
source: Although these LC3-labeled tubules were not associated with ER or actin filaments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), a portion of them tightly colocalized with microtubules stained for Tubulin (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: A portion of LC3-labeled tubules in TBC1D15−/− cells tightly colocalized with microtubules stained for Tubulin.
source: Although these LC3-labeled tubules were not associated with ER or actin filaments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), a portion of them tightly colocalized with microtubules stained for Tubulin (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: LC3-labeled tubular structures and LC3 accumulation in TBC1D15−/− cells completely disappeared upon nocodazole treatment.
source: Although WT cells have similar LC3 puncta with or without nocodazole treatment, LC3-labeled tubular structures and LC3 accumulation in TBC1D15−/− cells completely disappeared upon nocodazole treatment (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Intact microtubules are essential for LC3-labeled membrane expansion in TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: Thus, intact microtubules are essential for LC3-labeled membrane expansion in TBC1D15−/− cells, a step upstream of autophagosome fusion with lysosomes where previous work indicated dynein-facilitated autophagy (Kimura et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is inferred from nocodazole treatment experiments and supported by cited literature.

claim: Some late endosomes/lysosomes colocalize with LC3 in TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: Although some late endosomes/lysosomes colocalize with LC3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) consistent with the results of immunoelectron microscopy (Figure 2G, panel f), the morphologies of lysosomes and the Golgi apparatus were similar between WT and TBC1D15−/− cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2G.

claim: The morphologies of lysosomes and the Golgi apparatus were similar between WT and TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: Although some late endosomes/lysosomes colocalize with LC3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) consistent with the results of immunoelectron microscopy (Figure 2G, panel f), the morphologies of lysosomes and the Golgi apparatus were similar between WT and TBC1D15−/− cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: More endogenous lipidated LC3 (LC3-II) accumulated in TBC1D15−/− cells as compared to that of WT cells as also seen in FIS1−/− cells.
source: More endogenous lipidated LC3 (LC3-II) accumulated in TBC1D15−/− cells as compared to that of WT cells as also seen in FIS1−/− cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mfn1 was completely degraded within 2 hr in WT, FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: Although Mfn1, a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, was completely degraded within 2 hr in WT, FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells, ubiquitination of TOMM20, another outer membrane protein was retarded in FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells (Figure 4A; TOMM20 asterisk).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ubiquitination of TOMM20 was retarded in FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: Although Mfn1, a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, was completely degraded within 2 hr in WT, FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells, ubiquitination of TOMM20, another outer membrane protein was retarded in FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells (Figure 4A; TOMM20 asterisk).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PINK1 accumulates on the outer membrane upon addition of valinomycin.
source: In WT cells, PINK1 is barely detectable under normal growing conditions because of the degradation through N-end rule pathway (Yamano and Youle, 2013), whereas it accumulates on the outer membrane upon addition of valinomycin (Figure 4A) as seen also with CCCP (Matsuda et al., 2010; Vives-Bauza et al., 2010; Narendra et al., 2010b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A and cited literature.

claim: Accumulated PINK1 in FIS1−/− or TBC1D15−/− was retained longer than in WT cells.
source: On the other hand, accumulated PINK1 in FIS1−/− or TBC1D15−/− was retained longer than in WT cells (Figure 4A), suggesting, in conjunction with the delayed TOMM20 degradation, that autophagic clearance and/or proteasomal degradation is delayed in FIS1−/− or TBC1D15−/− cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Autophagic clearance and/or proteasomal degradation is delayed in FIS1−/− or TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: On the other hand, accumulated PINK1 in FIS1−/− or TBC1D15−/− was retained longer than in WT cells (Figure 4A), suggesting, in conjunction with the delayed TOMM20 degradation, that autophagic clearance and/or proteasomal degradation is delayed in FIS1−/− or TBC1D15−/− cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing delayed degradation of mitochondrial proteins.

claim: The rate of degradation of TOMM20, TIMM23, and mitochondrial HSP60 in FIS1−/− or TBC1D15−/− cells was not different as compared to that of WT cells at the 8-hr time points.
source: The rate of degradation of TOMM20, TIMM23, and mitochondrial HSP60 in FIS1−/− or TBC1D15−/− cells, however, was not different as compared to that of WT cells at the 8-hr time points (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When cells were treated with valinomycin for longer times up to 40 hr, most of the TOMM20 was degraded and protein levels of the matrix HSP60 and the mitochondrial DNA-encoded COXII (MT-COXII) decreased in WT cells, whereas they were retained in FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: On the other hand, when cells were treated with valinomycin for longer times up to 40 hr, most of the TOMM20 was degraded and protein levels of the matrix HSP60 and the mitochondrial DNA-encoded COXII (MT-COXII) decreased in WT cells, whereas they were retained in FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The Fis1-TBC1D15 pair is not essential for mitophagy but the deletion of either impedes clearance of damaged mitochondria.
source: These results indicate that the Fis1-TBC1D15 pair is not essential for mitophagy but the deletion of either impedes clearance of damaged mitochondria, despite the greater magnitude of LC3 accumulation following Parkin translocation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing delayed but not absent mitochondrial degradation in FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells.

claim: Fis1 is degraded during mitophagy, but TBC1D15 escapes the degradation.
source: We also found that, although Fis1 is degraded during mitophagy, TBC1D15 escapes the degradation (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The excessively long mitochondria found in MFF−/− or DRP−/− cells are converted from an elongated tubular network to larger, more rounded, or bubble-like structures relative to WT cells upon 3 hr valinomycin treatment.
source: The excessively long mitochondria found in MFF−/− or DRP−/− cells are converted from an elongated tubular network to larger, more rounded, or bubble-like structures relative to WT cells upon 3 hr valinomycin treatment (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Parkin translocation and mitochondrial colocalization with YFP-LC3 in MFF−/− and DRP1−/− cells were similar to those in WT cells without the LC3 accumulation and/or tubulation seen in FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: However, Parkin translocation and mitochondrial colocalization with YFP-LC3 in MFF−/− and DRP1−/− cells were similar to those in WT cells (Figure 5A–C) without the LC3 accumulation and/or tubulation seen in FIS1−/− and TBC1D15−/− cells (Figure 2A and Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: LC3 accumulation is a unique feature following the loss of Fis1 or TBC1D15 and is not caused by defects in mitochondrial fission.
source: These results suggest that LC3 accumulation is a unique feature following the loss of Fis1 or TBC1D15 and is not caused by defects in mitochondrial fission, consistent with the finding that Fis1 and TBC1D15 do not appear to regulate mitochondrial morphology (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing no LC3 accumulation in MFF−/− and DRP1−/− cells despite fission defects.

claim: Upon starvation, the number of YFP-LC3 puncta greatly increased, but indistinguishably between WT, FIS1−/−, and TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: Upon starvation, the number of YFP-LC3 puncta greatly increased, but indistinguishably between WT, FIS1−/−, and TBC1D15−/− cells (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Although more of the lipidated LC3 was generated upon starvation, the amount was not further increased by the depletion of Fis1 or TBC1D15.
source: Additionally, immunoblotting of endogenous LC3 demonstrated that although more of the lipidated LC3 was generated upon starvation, the amount was not further increased by the depletion of Fis1 or TBC1D15 (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: TBC1D15 and Fis1, which form a complex on mitochondria, seem to govern autophagosome biogenesis specifically during mitophagy.
source: Therefore, TBC1D15 and Fis1, which form a complex on mitochondria, seem to govern autophagosome biogenesis specifically during mitophagy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing no effect on starvation-induced autophagy but effects on mitophagy.

claim: Mitochondrial localization of TBC1D15 Δ221-250 was observed under normal growing conditions.
source: Unexpectedly, mitochondrial localization of TBC1D15 Δ221-250 was observed under normal growing conditions (Figure 6A) and HA-TBC1D15 Δ221-250 could rescue LC3 accumulation in TBC1D15−/− cells during mitophagy (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: HA-TBC1D15 Δ221-250 could rescue LC3 accumulation in TBC1D15−/− cells during mitophagy.
source: Unexpectedly, mitochondrial localization of TBC1D15 Δ221-250 was observed under normal growing conditions (Figure 6A) and HA-TBC1D15 Δ221-250 could rescue LC3 accumulation in TBC1D15−/− cells during mitophagy (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: In a FIS1−/− background, TBC1D15 localizes to the cytosol.
source: However, TBC1D15 appears to bind Fis1 as reported (Onoue et al., 2013) because in a FIS1−/− background, TBC1D15 localizes to the cytosol (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and cited literature.

claim: Fis1 overexpression can recruit overexpressed cytosolic WT TBC1D15, but not TBC1D15 Δ221-250, to the mitochondria.
source: Furthermore, Fis1 overexpression can recruit overexpressed cytosolic WT TBC1D15, but not TBC1D15 Δ221-250, to the mitochondria (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There is another protein that can facilitate TBC1D15 Δ221-250 binding to Fis1.
source: These results raise the possibility that there is another protein that can facilitate TBC1D15 Δ221-250 binding to Fis1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that TBC1D15 Δ221-250 localizes to mitochondria despite lacking the Fis1-binding region.

claim: TBC1D17 has a high similarity to the primary protein sequence of TBC1D15.
source: According to phylogenetic and domain analysis of human and mouse TBC proteins (Itoh et al., 2006), TBC1D17 has a high similarity to the primary protein sequence of TBC1D15.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The region outside the TBC domain comprising 193-312 aa of TBC1D17 is 35% identical (55% positive) to the 201-333 aa region of TBC1D15 that contains the Fis1-interacting region.
source: Specifically, the region outside the TBC domain comprising 193-312 aa of TBC1D17 is 35% identical (55% positive) to the 201-333 aa region of TBC1D15 that contains the Fis1-interacting region (data not shown), suggesting that TBC1D17 may also interact with Fis1.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data.

claim: TBC1D17 may also interact with Fis1.
source: Specifically, the region outside the TBC domain comprising 193-312 aa of TBC1D17 is 35% identical (55% positive) to the 201-333 aa region of TBC1D15 that contains the Fis1-interacting region (data not shown), suggesting that TBC1D17 may also interact with Fis1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from sequence similarity and supported by experimental data.

claim: Overexpressed HA-TBC1D17 alone was cytosolic.
source: Overexpressed HA-TBC1D17 alone was cytosolic (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: After co-overexpression with Fis1, HA-TBC1D17 localized to mitochondria.
source: However, after co-overexpression with Fis1, HA-TBC1D17 localized to mitochondria (Figure 6C), indicating that like TBC1D15, TBC1D17 has an ability to bind Fis1.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Like TBC1D15, TBC1D17 has an ability to bind Fis1.
source: However, after co-overexpression with Fis1, HA-TBC1D17 localized to mitochondria (Figure 6C), indicating that like TBC1D15, TBC1D17 has an ability to bind Fis1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from microscopy data and supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 can form homo- and hetero-dimers.
source: By co-immunoprecipitation, we found that TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 can form homo- and hetero-dimers (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The TBC1D15 Δ221-250 mutant that lacks a Fis1-binding region translocates to mitochondria when co-overexpressed with Fis1 and WT TBC1D15 or WT TBC1D17.
source: Furthermore, the TBC1D15 Δ221-250 mutant that lacks a Fis1-binding region translocates to mitochondria when co-overexpressed with Fis1 and WT TBC1D15 or WT TBC1D17 (Figure 6F), indicating that TBC1D17 can recruit the mutant TBC1D15 to Fis1 through dimerization.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: TBC1D17 can recruit the mutant TBC1D15 to Fis1 through dimerization.
source: Furthermore, the TBC1D15 Δ221-250 mutant that lacks a Fis1-binding region translocates to mitochondria when co-overexpressed with Fis1 and WT TBC1D15 or WT TBC1D17 (Figure 6F), indicating that TBC1D17 can recruit the mutant TBC1D15 to Fis1 through dimerization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing rescue of TBC1D15 Δ221-250 localization.

claim: Fis1 also forms dimers.
source: These results are also interesting in light of evidence that Fis1 also forms dimers (Jofuku et al., 2005; Lees et al., 2012) suggesting a new model of Fis1/TBC topology (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TBC1D17 single KO and TBC1D15/TBC1D17 double KO (DKO) HCT116 cells were generated by the TALEN methodology.
source: To examine the functional importance of TBC1D17 in mitophagy, we generated TBC1D17 single KO and TBC1D15/TBC1D17 double KO (DKO) HCT116 cells by the TALEN methodology (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mitochondrial and peroxisomal morphologies in TBC1D17−/− and TBC1D15/TBC1D17 DKO cells were indistinguishable from those in WT cells.
source: Mitochondrial and peroxisomal morphologies in these cells were indistinguishable from those in WT cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: TBC1D17−/− cells displayed LC3 accumulation during mitophagy similar to, but less severe than that of TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: TBC1D17−/− cells displayed LC3 accumulation during mitophagy similar to, but less severe than that of TBC1D15−/− cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: The degree of LC3 accumulation in TBC1D15/TBC1D17 DKO cells was not further increased as compared to that of TBC1D15 single KO.
source: However, the degree of LC3 accumulation in TBC1D15/TBC1D17 DKO cells was not further increased as compared to that of TBC1D15 single KO.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data.

claim: In HCT116 cells, TBC1D15 appears to be dominant for contouring autophagosome morphogenesis.
source: Therefore, in HCT116 cells, TBC1D15 appears to be dominant for contouring autophagosome morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing no additive effect in DKO cells.

claim: Overexpression of either TBC1D15 or TBC1D17 can rescue the LC3 accumulation in TBC1D15/17DKO cells, whereas the TBC1D15 Δ221-250 mutant cannot.
source: Overexpression of either TBC1D15 or TBC1D17 can rescue the LC3 accumulation in TBC1D15/17DKO cells, whereas the TBC1D15 Δ221-250 mutant cannot (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: Fis1 binding is required for TBC1D15 to govern isolation membrane biogenesis during mitophagy.
source: Thus, Fis1 binding is required for TBC1D15 to govern isolation membrane biogenesis during mitophagy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from rescue experiments showing the TBC1D15 Δ221-250 mutant cannot rescue LC3 accumulation.

claim: YFP-GABARAPL1 forms massively expanded structures in FIS1−/− and in TBC1D15−/− cells after Parkin translocation induced by valinomycin treatment.
source: Similar to YFP-LC3B (Figure 2A), YFP-GABARAPL1 also forms massively expanded structures in FIS1−/− and in TBC1D15−/− cells after Parkin translocation induced by valinomycin treatment (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: LC3 and GABARAP subfamily members bind in moderate and high amounts to YFP-TBC1D15, respectively.
source: While GST alone does not bind YFP-TBC1D15, LC3, and GABARAP subfamily members bind in moderate and high amounts to YFP-TBC1D15, respectively (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Fis1 cannot bind GABARAPL1.
source: Fis1 cannot bind GABARAPL1, confirming that the binding between TBC1D15 and GABARAPL1 is not mediated indirectly through Fis1 (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The GABARAPL1 LDS mutant failed to bind YFP-TBC1D15.
source: Although equal amounts of GST-tagged GABARAPL1 WT and LDS mutant were expressed and immunoprecipitated, the LDS mutant failed to bind YFP-TBC1D15 (Figure 7C), indicating that the binding occurs through LIR–LDS interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The binding between TBC1D15 and GABARAPL1 occurs through LIR–LDS interactions.
source: Although equal amounts of GST-tagged GABARAPL1 WT and LDS mutant were expressed and immunoprecipitated, the LDS mutant failed to bind YFP-TBC1D15 (Figure 7C), indicating that the binding occurs through LIR–LDS interactions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mutational analysis data.

claim: Only the 201–333 region of TBC1D15 retained the affinity for GABARAPL1.
source: Transiently overexpressed TBC1D15 domains in HEK293 cells subjected to in vitro binding assays revealed that only the 201–333 region retained the affinity for GABARAPL1 (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: 280FEVI283 of TBC1D15 is the LIR motif responsible for full length TBC1D15 binding to GABARAPL1.
source: By mutating the aromatic amino acid in each of these five LIR candidates to alanine, we identified 280FEVI283 of TBC1D15 as the LIR motif responsible for full length TBC1D15 binding to GABARAPL1 (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by mutational analysis data shown in Figure 7G,H.

claim: The LC3 membrane accumulation phenotype of the TBC1D15−/− cells was only partially rescued by the TBC1D15 F280A mutant.
source: The LC3 membrane accumulation phenotype of the TBC1D15−/− cells was only partially rescued by the TBC1D15 F280A mutant (Figure 7J,K) relative to the complete rescue seen with WT TBC1D15, indicating that the interaction between TBC1D15 and Atg8 family proteins is important for autophagosome morphogenesis during Parkin-mediated mitophagy.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 7J,K.

claim: The interaction between TBC1D15 and Atg8 family proteins is important for autophagosome morphogenesis during Parkin-mediated mitophagy.
source: The LC3 membrane accumulation phenotype of the TBC1D15−/− cells was only partially rescued by the TBC1D15 F280A mutant (Figure 7J,K) relative to the complete rescue seen with WT TBC1D15, indicating that the interaction between TBC1D15 and Atg8 family proteins is important for autophagosome morphogenesis during Parkin-mediated mitophagy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from rescue experiment data.

claim: Amino acids 261–264 of TBC1D17 are identical to the sequence of the LIR motif in TBC1D15 (FEVI).
source: Interestingly, amino acids 261–264 of TBC1D17 are identical to the sequence of the LIR motif in TBC1D15 (FEVI) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence comparison data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Both LC3 and GABARAP subfamilies pulled down YFP-TBC1D17.
source: Both LC3 and GABARAP subfamilies pulled down YFP-TBC1D17 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B), and this interaction was mediated by the LDS domain of ATG8 family proteins (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,D) with less discrimination between GABARAP and LC3 subfamily members than TBC1D15 (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The interaction between TBC1D17 and ATG8 family proteins was mediated by the LDS domain of ATG8 family proteins.
source: Both LC3 and GABARAP subfamilies pulled down YFP-TBC1D17 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B), and this interaction was mediated by the LDS domain of ATG8 family proteins (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,D) with less discrimination between GABARAP and LC3 subfamily members than TBC1D15 (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: The LIR mutation F261A prevented binding of TBC1D17 to GST-LC3B.
source: Furthermore, the LIR mutation F261A prevented binding of TBC1D17 to GST-LC3B (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Both TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 have the ability to bind ATG8 family proteins via a LIR–LDS interaction.
source: These results indicate that both TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 have the ability to bind ATG8 family proteins via a LIR–LDS interaction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing LIR-dependent binding.

claim: In vitro GTPase assays and pull-down assays in cells suggest that TBC1D15 may function as a Rab-GAP for Rab7.
source: Although little is known about the pairing between various Rab proteins and TBC proteins, in vitro GTPase assays (Zhang et al., 2005) and pull-down assays in cells (Peralta et al., 2010) suggest that TBC1D15 may function as a Rab-GAP for Rab7.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Rab7 is required for endosome maturation and transport from the late endosome to the lysosome.
source: Rab7 is required for endosome maturation and transport from the late endosome to the lysosome (Bento et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Rab7 has been reported to be involved in the biogenesis of autophagosomes.
source: However, Rab7 also has been reported to be involved in the biogenesis of autophagosomes (Gutierrez et al., 2004; Jager et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Two Rab7 siRNAs were able to completely suppress the abnormal LC3 accumulation and tubulation in both FIS1−/− or TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: These two Rab7 siRNAs were able to completely suppress the abnormal LC3 accumulation and tubulation in both FIS1−/− or TBC1D15−/− cells (Figure 8B,C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 8B,C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: After 3 hr valinomycin treatment of WT cells, 2HA-Rab7 colocalized with some of the YFP-LC3 in WT cells in dot or crescent-shaped structures that represent isolation membranes.
source: However, after 3 hr valinomycin treatment of WT cells, 2HA-Rab7 colocalized with some of the YFP-LC3 in WT cells in dot or crescent-shaped structures that represent isolation membranes, indicating that Rab7 is targeted to isolation membranes upon stimulation of mitophagy (Figure 8D, WT valinomycin).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Rab7 is targeted to isolation membranes upon stimulation of mitophagy.
source: However, after 3 hr valinomycin treatment of WT cells, 2HA-Rab7 colocalized with some of the YFP-LC3 in WT cells in dot or crescent-shaped structures that represent isolation membranes, indicating that Rab7 is targeted to isolation membranes upon stimulation of mitophagy (Figure 8D, WT valinomycin).
evidence: The claim is inferred from microscopy data showing Rab7 colocalization with LC3.

claim: Rab7 was found on YFP-LC3 positive tubules in TBC1D15−/− cells.
source: Interestingly, Rab7 was also found on YFP-LC3 positive tubules in TBC1D15−/− cells (Figure 8D, TBC1D15−/− valinomycin), strongly supporting the hypothesis that Rab7 functions in isolation membrane expansion during mitophagy.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Rab7 functions in isolation membrane expansion during mitophagy.
source: Interestingly, Rab7 was also found on YFP-LC3 positive tubules in TBC1D15−/− cells (Figure 8D, TBC1D15−/− valinomycin), strongly supporting the hypothesis that Rab7 functions in isolation membrane expansion during mitophagy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from microscopy data and siRNA experiments.

claim: HA-TBC1D15 D397A fails to rescue the accumulation of LC3 in TBC1D15−/− cells as WT TBC1D15 does.
source: Although HA-TBC1D15 D397A localizes on mitochondria (data not shown), it fails to rescue the accumulation of LC3 in TBC1D15−/− cells as WT TBC1D15 does (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 8E,F.

claim: Overexpression of TBC1D17 catalytic mutant R381A could not rescue the LC3 accumulation in the TBC1D15/TBC1D17 DKO cells.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of TBC1D17 catalytic mutant R381A could not rescue the LC3 accumulation in the TBC1D15/TBC1D17 DKO cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Rab7 siRNA could suppress YFP-LC3 accumulation in TBC1D17−/− cells.
source: Although many different Rab proteins such as Rab5, Rab8, Rab21 and Rab35 have been suggested to be the targets of TBC1D17 (Itoh et al., 2006; Fuchs et al., 2007; Vaibhava et al., 2012), Rab7 siRNA could suppress YFP-LC3 accumulation in TBC1D17−/− cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Rab-GAP activity inhibits Rab7 to mitigate excessive autophagosome membrane expansion during mitophagy.
source: These results support the model that Rab-GAP activity inhibits Rab7 to mitigate excessive autophagosome membrane expansion during mitophagy and, through Fis1 binding to mitochondria and LC3 family member binding on isolation membranes, tailors the autophagosomal membrane expansion to its cargo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing the requirement for GAP activity and Rab7 involvement.

claim: Through Fis1 binding to mitochondria and LC3 family member binding on isolation membranes, TBC1D15/17 tailors the autophagosomal membrane expansion to its cargo.
source: These results support the model that Rab-GAP activity inhibits Rab7 to mitigate excessive autophagosome membrane expansion during mitophagy and, through Fis1 binding to mitochondria and LC3 family member binding on isolation membranes, tailors the autophagosomal membrane expansion to its cargo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing the requirement for both Fis1 and LC3 binding.

claim: Rab7, TBC1D15 and TBC1D17, and Fis1 are mitophagy effectors functioning downstream of Parkin to regulate autophagosome morphogenesis.
source: In this study, we identify Rab7, TBC1D15 and TBC1D17, and Fis1 as mitophagy effectors functioning downstream of Parkin to regulate autophagosome morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: PINK1 accumulates on the outer membrane of depolarized mitochondria and recruits Parkin and activates Parkin ubiquitin ligase activity.
source: As PINK1 accumulates on the outer membrane of depolarized mitochondria, it recruits Parkin and activates Parkin ubiquitin ligase activity (Iguchi et al., 2013; Lazarou et al., 2013; Zheng and Hunter, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Parkin modifies numerous mitochondrial outer membrane proteins with K48- and K63-linked ubiquitin chains.
source: Parkin then modifies numerous mitochondrial outer membrane proteins with K48- and K63-linked ubiquitin chains.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The ubiquitin signal appears to recruit ULK1, Atg9 and LC3 to the mitochondrion independently of one another to induce mitophagy.
source: This ubiquitin signal appears to recruit ULK1, Atg9 and LC3 to the mitochondrion independently of one another to induce mitophagy (Itakura et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Rab7 is likely activated by a Rab GEF to promote autophagosomal membrane growth and microtubule associated trafficking.
source: Our results also indicate that Rab7 is likely activated by a Rab GEF to promote autophagosomal membrane growth and microtubule associated trafficking and that TBC1D15/17 Rab GAP activity is required to temper Rab7 activity to tailor autophagosomal membrane expansion to surround mitochondrial aggregates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing Rab7 involvement and the requirement for GAP activity.

claim: TBC1D15/17 Rab GAP activity is required to temper Rab7 activity to tailor autophagosomal membrane expansion to surround mitochondrial aggregates.
source: Our results also indicate that Rab7 is likely activated by a Rab GEF to promote autophagosomal membrane growth and microtubule associated trafficking and that TBC1D15/17 Rab GAP activity is required to temper Rab7 activity to tailor autophagosomal membrane expansion to surround mitochondrial aggregates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing the requirement for GAP activity.

claim: Without TBC1D15, or with TBC1D15 lacking Rab GAP activity, LC3/GABARAP-labeled isolation membranes accumulate excessively and without cargo orientation sending long tubules away from mitochondria along microtubule tracks.
source: Without TBC1D15, or with TBC1D15 lacking Rab GAP activity, LC3/GABARAP-labeled isolation membranes accumulate excessively and without cargo orientation sending long tubules away from mitochondria along microtubule tracks.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing LC3 accumulation and tubulation in TBC1D15−/− cells.

claim: Rab GAP activity localized on the cargo—facing only one side of the expanding LC3 positive isolation membranes—may inhibit Rab7 activity and thereby inhibit membrane expansion proximal to the cargo forcing the growing membrane to tightly wrap odd shaped cargo.
source: This suggests that Rab GAP activity localized on the cargo—facing only one side of the expanding LC3 positive isolation membranes—may inhibit Rab7 activity and thereby inhibit membrane expansion proximal to the cargo forcing the growing membrane to tightly wrap odd shaped cargo.
evidence: The claim is a speculative model based on experimental data.

claim: LC3-decorated preautophagosomal structures may traffic along microtubules toward Parkin-ubiquitinated mitochondria and fuse together around mitochondrial aggregates where TBC1D15 bound to mitochondria inhibits Rab7 to mediate the release of LC3-bound membranes from microtubules as they contact the mitochondrial cargo.
source: Alternatively, perhaps LC3-decorated preautophagosomal structures traffic along microtubules toward Parkin-ubiquitinated mitochondria and fuse together around mitochondrial aggregates where TBC1D15 bound to mitochondria inhibits Rab7 to mediate the release of LC3-bound membranes from microtubules as they contact the mitochondrial cargo (Pankiv et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is a speculative model based on experimental data and cited literature.

claim: TBC1D15−/− cells display normal LC3 accumulation during starvation suggesting that these membrane expansion steps are specific for mitophagy or other forms of selective autophagy.
source: TBC1D15−/− cells display normal LC3 accumulation during starvation suggesting that these membrane expansion steps are specific for mitophagy or other forms of selective autophagy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing no effect on starvation-induced autophagy.

claim: Xenophagy requires Rab proteins for sequestering invading bacteria in autophagosome-like vacuoles.
source: Xenophagy, for example, also requires Rab proteins for sequestering invading bacteria in autophagosome-like vacuoles (Yamaguchi et al., 2009), consistent with the idea that isolation membrane expansion is mediated by Rab activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Parkin may activate Rab proteins as a step in xenophagy.
source: Parkin also may activate Rab proteins as a step in xenophagy (Manzanillo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: An LIR domain in TBC1D15, conserved in TBC1D17, is required to restrain isolation membrane biogenesis to the surface of the mitochondria.
source: We identify an LIR domain in TBC1D15, conserved in TBC1D17, that is also required to restrain isolation membrane biogenesis to the surface of the mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the importance of the LIR domain.

claim: TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 appear to constitutively bind to mitochondria through Fis1 and thus would not appear to initiate the recruitment of LC3 to mitochondria.
source: However, in contrast to the ubiquitin-binding LIR domain proteins, TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 appear to constitutively bind to mitochondria through Fis1 and thus, unless somehow regulated, would not appear to initiate the recruitment of LC3 to mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing constitutive mitochondrial localization.

claim: TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 use LC3/GABARAP binding in the context of Rab GAP activity to orient growing isolation membranes to the surface of the cargo.
source: More likely, TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 use LC3/GABARAP binding in the context of Rab GAP activity to orient growing isolation membranes to the surface of the cargo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing the requirement for both LC3 binding and GAP activity.

claim: TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 appear to heterodimerize and homodimerize, which may increase their affinity for LC3/GABARAP by multivalent binding.
source: Interestingly, TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 appear to heterodimerize and homodimerize, which may increase their affinity for LC3/GABARAP by multivalent binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The self association of TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 is shared by other ubiquitin-binding LIR domain proteins such as p62.
source: The self association of TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 is shared by other ubiquitin-binding LIR domain proteins such as p62 (Birgisdottir et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Dnm1 activity in yeast and Drp1 activity in mammalian cells is required for mitophagy.
source: Interestingly, Dnm1 activity in yeast (Mao et al., 2013), and Drp1 activity in mammalian cells is required for mitophagy (Twig et al., 2008; Tanaka et al., 2010; Frank et al., 2012) suggesting a link with Fis1 in mitophagy.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Yeast Fis1 has an N-terminal extension that folds back into a pocket used by other tetratricopeptide motif proteins to bind ligands.
source: In contrast to human Fis1, yeast Fis1 has an N-terminal extension that folds back into a pocket used by other tetratricopeptide motif proteins to bind ligands (Suzuki et al., 2003, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Fis1 also localizes to peroxisomes and would be predicted to recruit TBC1D15/17 to peroxisomes as well, suggesting that Fis1 and TBC1D15/17 may also play a role in pexophagy.
source: Fis1 also localizes to peroxisomes and would be predicted to recruit TBC1D15/17 to peroxisomes as well, suggesting that Fis1 and TBC1D15/17 may also play a role in pexophagy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing Fis1 localization to peroxisomes.
